items.stem: Under the cost-to-cost method, progress is measured as:

options.text: Costs incurred to date divided by total estimated costs
options.rationale: Correct: cost-to-cost expresses progress as costs incurred over total estimated costs.

options.text: Cash received divided by contract price
options.rationale: Cash receipts do not measure progress.

options.text: Months elapsed divided by total months
options.rationale: Elapsed time is not the cost-to-cost measure.
Billings are not a progress measure under cost-to-cost.

items.explanation: Correct: cost-to-cost progress is costs incurred to date divided by total estimated costs.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: A contract is now expected to make an overall loss. Which TWO actions are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Recognise the entire expected loss immediately
options.rationale: Correct: an expected contract loss is recognised in full at once.

options.text: Reassess the cost-to-complete estimate that produced the loss
options.rationale: Correct: the estimate should be validated as part of recognising the loss.

options.text: Spread the loss evenly over the remaining term
options.rationale: Expected losses are not spread; they are recognised immediately.

options.text: Defer the loss until the contract ends
options.rationale: Deferring a known loss is not permitted.

items.explanation: Correct: an expected loss is recognised immediately after validating the cost-to-complete estimate.

items.stem: A revision to the estimated total cost of a contract is accounted for as:

options.text: A change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively through a cumulative catch-up
options.rationale: Correct: estimate revisions are prospective with a cumulative catch-up to revenue/margin.
A genuine estimate change is not an error.
It is a change in estimate, not policy.
The revision is reflected in the current period.

items.explanation: Correct: a change in cost estimate is treated prospectively with a cumulative catch-up.
